Operator:
    Good morning, and welcome to the AeroDef Technologies Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing and asking questions will be provided at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

    I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
    Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to AeroDef Technologies' Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are David Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; John Harlan, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer; and Dr. Michael Voss, Chief Technology Officer.

    Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Actual results may differ materially due to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of these factors.

David Reynolds:
    Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. AeroDef Technologies delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across commercial aerospace, defense systems, and high-margin services. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering long-term value to our shareholders. Today, we will cover several key areas: the discussion of geopolitical factors affecting defense spending; program margins and cost performance analysis; drivers of aftermarket performance such as fleet utilization and maintenance cycles; revenue by segment for commercial aerospace, defense, and services including year-over-year percentage changes; and the key assumptions underlying our guidance.

    We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our Viperstrike hypersonic glide vehicle program and its potential to accelerate our future growth through long-range strike capabilities and integration into multi-domain operations. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, including precision munitions and C4ISR platforms, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily with increased deliveries and aftermarket activity.

    With that, let me turn it over to John for a deeper dive into these topics and our financial results.

John Harlan:
    Thank you, David, and good morning, everyone. Let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $22.4 billion, representing an 18% increase year-over-year. Our adjusted earnings per share were $3.20, up 25% from the prior year. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $5.2 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at $28.5 to $29.5 billion in revenue and $12.80 to $13.20 in adjusted EPS. We are actively managing our costs, investing in key growth initiatives like digital transformation and supply chain reshoring, and focused on returning capital to shareholders through our quarterly dividend and ongoing share repurchase program, with $1.5 billion authorized remaining.

    Our specific financial highlights include a gross margin of 28%, up 150 basis points year-over-year; operating income of $2.8 billion, reflecting strong flow-through; and free cash flow of $1.2 billion for the quarter.

    Building on David's overview, let me provide more detail on those key areas starting with the geopolitical factors shaping defense spending, which are creating structural tailwinds for our industry. As a leader in next-generation aerospace platforms, precision munitions, and C4ISR systems—such as our Viperstrike hypersonic glide vehicle, the Block IV Shadowhawk UAV swarm, and our contributions to the F-35 Lightning II sustainment—these dynamics have accelerated our backlog to $148 billion, up 14% year-over-year.

    Globally, defense spending reached $2.24 trillion in 2023 according to SIPRI, a 6.8% real-term increase—the largest since the end of the Cold War—and we project a 4-5% compound annual growth rate through 2028 driven by multi-domain threats. In the U.S., the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act authorized $886 billion for the Department of Defense, 4.2% above FY2023 levels, with procurement and R&D rising 7.1% to $167 billion. This directly benefits programs like ours: our missile and munitions segment jumped 22% quarter-over-quarter from JASSM-ER and LRASM replenishment contracts tied to Ukraine inventory drawdowns. We've shipped over 1,200 all-up-rounds this year, and with the DoD invoking the Defense Production Act, we're doubling production to 150 units per month by Q1 2025.

    In Europe, the Russia-Ukraine war continues to drive urgency. NATO allies have provided €230 billion in aid since February 2022, with Ukraine using 90,000 artillery rounds monthly—far exceeding pre-war output. This has sparked rearmament: 23 of 32 NATO members now hit or exceed the 2% GDP target, up from just 9 in 2014. Poland's budget swelled 75% to $38 billion, securing our Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors and HIMARS variants. Germany's €100 billion Zeitenwende fund is 85% committed, favoring air defense like our Skyguard laser systems. We've landed €450 million in orders from the EUMAM Ukraine effort, lifting international backlog to 42% of total, with integrated air and missile defense demand growing 18% annually as allies blend U.S. systems like Aegis Ashore with local platforms.

    In the Indo-Pacific, China's aggression—including over 180 Taiwan Strait incursions this year—has shifted priorities. The U.S. Pacific Deterrence Initiative got $9.1 billion in FY2024, up 12%, supporting hypersonic defenses and dispersed basing. Japan aims for 2% GDP spending by 2027 at $82 billion, while AUKUS partners Australia and the UK advance SSN-AUKUS subs and GCAP fighters. Viperstrike, with its 5,000+ km range and Mach 8+ speeds, fits ideally—we've captured $1.2 billion in FY24 awards from JADC2 demos. QUAD collaboration on drone swarms positions our Shadowhawk Block IV, enabling AI autonomy for 200+ units, in low-rate initial production with Indian Navy trials in Q4.

    Middle East volatility layers on: U.S. aid to Israel post-October 7 hit $17.9 billion, covering Iron Dome and F-35I upgrades where we supply 40% of sensor fusion avionics. Iran's proxies and Houthi attacks boosted counter-UAS and naval strike needs—Harpoon Block II+ sales to Saudi Arabia and UAE rose 35% with 500+ deliveries. Regional spend is up 9% to $200 billion, though supply risks like Chinese rare earths and Russian titanium loom. We've countered with $250 million in our Alabama foundry for 95% domestic airframe sourcing.

    These trends highlight three takeaways for AeroDef: first, peacetime budgets are now focused on munitions, with conflicts depleting 60% of U.S. long-range stocks, leading to a $28 billion supplemental and our alignment with the Munitions Industrial Base strategy for 3x precision-guided munitions output by 2026. Second, great power competition demands tech leaps in hypersonics, directed energy, and collaborative combat aircraft—our NGAD bid is active, backed by $450 million in AI/ML for 15% prototype margin gains. Third, alliances amplify via eased ITAR for AUKUS/QUAD, unlocking $50 billion over five years. Risks include U.S. election-year fiscal cuts to overseas contingency operations, but core topline growth stays at 5-7% for FY25.

    Overall, these shifts are redefining deterrence, positioning us for $28.5-29.5 billion FY24 revenue, 28% EBITDA margins, and 19% ROIC.

    Next, on program margins and cost performance. Our aerospace and defense segments posted consolidated operating margins of 11.6% in Q3, up 120 basis points year-over-year and 40 basis points sequentially. This extends three quarters of expansion, from a $450 million year-to-date drop in cost variances, higher full-rate production volumes, and digital productivity. Excluding a $120 million underrun on a legacy rotary-wing sustainment deal, core margins hit 11.2%, beating guidance.

    In Aeronautics (45% of backlog), margins reached 10.8%, up 150 basis points, led by our Liberty Eagle next-gen fighter equivalent at 9.7%—up from 8.4%—on Lot 16 LRIP deliveries. Cost performance index was 1.05 on material savings, recovering $180 million in estimate-at-completion via titanium and composites negotiations. Labor shortages linger, addressed by 15% overtime and 500 new apprentices by year-end. Commercial widebody freighter margins fell to 7.2% from certification delays and 12% avionics inflation; an engineering change request for wingbox redesign targets $90 million FY25 savings.

    Missiles & Defense hit 14.9%, up 200 basis points, with hypersonic interceptor at 15.8% and schedule performance index of 1.08 from White Sands tests. Unit costs fell 22% on the learning curve; Patriot SAM sustainment at 16.2% took a $35 million forward loss on fixed-price range-frequency updates. Segment CPI was 1.12, with -3.5% material variances from rare earth hedging. $50 million in additive manufacturing cut rocket motor lead times 40% and scrap 28%.

    Space Systems steady at 10.4%, with GPS III follow-on at 11.1% post-FRP, offset by $65 million classified SATCOM growth from thermal vacuum delays—now fixed via dual-sourcing. CPI rebounded to 0.98. Commercial LEO added $200 million at 12.5% via reusable launches.

    Rotary & Mission Systems at 12.3%, up 90 basis points, from $150 million Australian FMS underruns despite 8% Philly labor inflation.

    Cost deep dive: $620 million operations cash from savings, 35% ahead. Supply chain council with 250 tier-1s like Honeywell saved $300 million via should-cost and AI forecasting, netting 6.1% productivity over 4.2% inflation. Digital twins on 70% programs cut engineering changes 45%; MBSE reduced rework 22% for 50 basis point lift. Lean Six Sigma saved 1.1 million hours, sigma to 4.2.

    U.S. DoD at 11.1% margins on 85% volume; international at 13.7% up 180 basis points from $1.2 billion Middle East and $800 million Europe. APAC at 9.8% but AUKUS poised for $5 billion subs.

    Forward, $2.5 billion fixed-price dev exposed to labor; $125 billion backlog converts at 12%+. We target 95% award fees, 20% FFP shift post-LRIP. FY24 guide: Aeronautics 11-12%, Missiles 14.5-15.5%, consolidated 11.8-12.5%.

    Turning to drivers of aftermarket performance, which grew 18% to $2.8 billion—42% of top line—at 31.2% EBITDA margins, up 210 basis points. This reflects MRO, spares, and upgrades for our platforms.

    Fleet utilization is key: commercial traffic at 95% pre-pandemic per IATA, pushing narrowbody daily hours to 11.8 from 9.2, nearing 12.5 peak. LEAP-1A/1B on A320neo and GTF on A220 drove 22% engine MRO from LCCs like Ryanair, IndiGo. Defense flight hours up 14% to 1.2 million, boosting F-35 PBL at $450 million for 95% mission capability.

    Maintenance cycles align: commercial mid-life C/D-checks every 18-24 months post-deferred wear, up 15% heavy events; mobile teams at 12 sites. Margins to 28% via EHM on 85% CFM56/LEAP, cutting no-fault-founds 35%. Defense longevity like Super Hornet E-2D beyond 6,000 hours adds $300 million; conflicts spike F-15/Apache 25%, RAF Typhoon upgrades.

    North America 55% growth (KC-46, 787); Europe 25% (Lufthansa A350); Asia-Pac 30% (ANA/SIA 777X, Tejas); Middle East -5% offset by Dubai spares.

    Initiatives: digital twins on 70% defense engines for condition-based maintenance, +15-20% intervals, 500 bps margins. Additive for titanium cuts lead 120-to-14 days, 25% costs for F-35 Lots 15-17. TruePower at 60% on LEAP. $12-14 billion by 2027 at 10-12% growth, 200-300 bps accretion; $5.2 billion backlog, 98% retention.

    On revenue by segment: Commercial aerospace at $9.4 billion, 42% total, +28% YoY on narrowbody ramps (LEAP-1A 420 units +35%, $500 million San Diego titanium). Widebody +22% (787/A350, 777X $1.2 billion). Aftermarket +32% to $3.8 billion at 85% 2019 hours; Asia-Pac 40%, North America 25%. Boeing MAX caps, forging inflation offset by digital twins (15% less downtime, 28% MRO attach).

    Defense $8.5 billion, 38%, +12%: F-35 F135 $4.1 billion +18% (Lot 15/16); hypersonics $800 million +50%; rotary/ISR +9% (UH-60 T700). Middle East FMS 30%; services +14%. Margins 12.5%, Huntsville ramp for space payloads; 1.3x book-to-bill target.

    Services $4.5 billion, 20%, +22%: TotalCare/TrueChoice 65% base, EHM 25% uptake ($250 million AOG savings). Commercial 787/777X, defense F-16/P-8. APAC +28%, EMEA +20%. $300 million SAF/hybrid for X-66A. Dual-source 80% composites, hedge 70% TiAl. FY25: commercial 25-30%, defense 10-12%, services 20%+; margins +150 bps to 14.5%.

    Finally, key assumptions for FY25 guidance: revenue $28.5-29.5 billion (7-10% organic), EPS $12.80-13.20, margins 13.0-13.5%, FCF $3.2-3.5 billion (110-115% conversion), 1.1x book-to-bill on $52 billion funded backlog.

    Aeronautics (45%): 12-15% commercial OEM on 550-600 737/A320neo deliveries; 8% MRO at 85% utilization. Defense F-35 Lot 17/18 156 aircraft, $4.2 billion sustainment (90-day TR-3 slips max), NGAD $800 million ($2.5 billion AF request). Europe +15% F-35, EASA slips <60 days.

    Missiles & Space (35%): 10-12% on $5.2 billion DoD hypersonics (ARRW FRP, Black Widow), $3.1 billion missiles (1,200 PAC-3), 2% Glide Phase overrun max. Space $2.8 billion (GPS IIIF SV-08-12 Vulcan Q1, STPSat-6 $450 million), commercial SATCOM +5% (two Falcon slips/quarter max). Asia-Pac 30%, Middle East flat $900 million.

    Integrated Defense (20%): 5-7% on Aegis SPY-6 $2.1 billion (1.5/month arrays), GMD $1.2 billion (20 GBIs). Digital twins/MBSE 25% hours for 15% Patriot savings. AUKUS $600 million, Saudi $3.5 billion.

    Macros: inflation 3.5-4% (Ti $25/kg, labor 4.2% offset 10% productivity via AeroForge 30% weight cuts); 95% tier-1 delivery (no Spirit delays), $200 million CHIPS fabs. FX EUR 1.08/GBP 1.25; FY25 omnibus March no extended CRs.

    Sensitivities: 1% revenue miss = $0.10 EPS; 100 bps inflation = $0.05. Upside: +$1 billion F-35/B-21; geopolitics +2%.

    This sets us up strongly on our backlog and tailwinds.

Lisa Chen:
    Thank you, John. Operationally, we've made significant strides in supply chain management, boosting production rates on key programs like Viperstrike and Shadowhawk. We've optimized with our Prime Supplier Council, achieving $300 million in savings through should-cost modeling and AI forecasting. Investments in automation, digital twins across 70% of programs, and additive manufacturing have enhanced efficiency, cutting lead times 40% and engineering changes 45%. We've ramped headcount 10% in critical areas like Huntsville and Alabama, ensuring 95% domestic sourcing amid global disruptions. These efforts, combined with Lean Six Sigma yielding 1.1 million saved hours, position us for sustained margin expansion and backlog execution.

Operator:
    Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Instructions for asking questions will be repeated if needed. Our first question comes from Josh Smith with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Josh Smith:
    Good morning, team. Can you provide more color on how specific geopolitical risks, like potential U.S. budget cuts or supply chain bottlenecks from China and Russia, might impact your international backlog?

David Reynolds:
    Good morning, Josh. Excellent question tying into our earlier discussion. While fiscal pressures in an election year could trim overseas contingency funding, our baseline U.S. topline remains resilient at 5-7% growth, supported by the FY24 NDAA's $886 billion. On supply, we've invested $250 million in Alabama for 95% domestic airframes, hedging rare earths and gallium ahead of restrictions, and dual-sourcing criticals. Our international backlog at 42%, including €450 million EUMAM and $1.2 billion Indo-Pacific, benefits from alliance easing like AUKUS ITAR—$50 billion opportunity. We're stress-testing for 10% export delays but see net tailwinds from munitions replenishments and rearmament.

Operator:
    Our next question comes from Emily Carter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter:
    Hi, thanks. On program margins, particularly in commercial aeronautics, what gives you confidence in recapturing to 11-12% FY24 amid certification delays and inflation?

John Harlan:
    Hi, Emily. Confidence stems from our EAC reductions—like $180 million on Liberty Eagle via supplier negotiations—and ECRs targeting $90 million wingbox savings. We've absorbed 15% overtime and launched apprenticeships for 500 machinists. Digital initiatives add 50 basis points: twins and MBSE cut rework 22%. Fixed-price shift post-LRIP and 95% award fees on CPIF mirror RTX success. Even with 12% avionics inflation, productivity at 6.1% outpaces 4.2% CPI. Peers like LMT guide lower; we're ahead.

Operator:
    Our next question comes from Raj Patel with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Raj Patel:
    Regarding the drivers of aftermarket performance, how sustainable is the 30% Asia-Pacific growth, and what tech levers like digital twins are key to margin upside?

Dr. Michael Voss:
    Raj, great to hear from you. Sustainability is strong: booming intra-Asia routes push A350/777X inductions for Qantas, Air India, with utilization to 85%. EHM on 85% LEAP/CFM56 cuts no-faults 35%, predictive algos extend intervals 15-20%. Digital twins on 70% engines shift to condition-based, unlocking 500 bps. Additive titanium for hot-sections: 14-day leads, 25% cheaper for F-35 quals. TruePower 60% attach derisks airlines. $120 billion TAM at 6-8% CAGR; our $5.2 billion backlog, 98% retention buffers FAA/GTF risks.

David Reynolds:
    Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, innovation in hypersonics and autonomy, and executing our $148 billion backlog.

Sarah Thompson:
    Thank you for joining us today. A replay of this call will be available on our investor relations website. This concludes our Q3 2024 earnings call.

Operator:
    This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
